strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving dense RGB-D SLAM with self-supervised visual features, without requiring task-specific semantic annotations or predefined object categories.

The proposed design is tested with both implicit NeRF/tri-plane and explicit 3D Gaussian representations. Additional integrations with hash grids, neural points, and semantic SLAM provide useful evidence that the idea is not tied to one particular map representation.

Evaluation covers synthetic and real-world benchmarks—Replica, ScanNet, and TUM—and considers reconstruction, rendering, tracking, runtime, and model size. Several results improve over the corresponding base systems, including completion and tracking for the ESLAM-based variant and average tracking error for the 3DGS variant.
The raw-DINO versus EDINO ablations indicate that the proposed feature fusion can improve upon directly using DINO features. Global bundle adjustment is also separately ablated for the 3DGS system.
The paper is visually clear, and its high-level pipeline, two representation variants, and main empirical findings are easy to follow.
weaknesses: No contribution type is declared, so I assess this as Algorithms/General. Under that framing, the technical specification is insufficient to establish soundness or reproducibility. In particular, the paper does not explain how pixel-aligned EDINO features are spatially aligned with and directly compared to three coordinate-plane tensors in Eq. 7, or how an EDINO feature is associated with each Gaussian. Eq. 10 remains an ordinary Gaussian equation despite the claim that EDINO is added to the Gaussian parameters. Tensor dimensions, feature layers, normalization, projection/back-projection, occlusion handling, and optimization schedules are largely absent.

The central claims of hierarchical scene understanding, part-whole relations, and scene-level layouts are not directly evaluated. All reported endpoints concern geometry, appearance, or trajectory accuracy; there are no feature-quality probes, correspondence tests, semantic/open-vocabulary evaluations, visualizations of the learned hierarchy, or controlled analyses showing that the attention operations actually capture the claimed structural relationships.

The gains are often small: for example, the Replica 3DGS improvements over MonoGS are 0.18 dB PSNR and 0.02 cm trajectory RMSE, and the TUM NeRF average improves over ESLAM by only 0.05 cm. Results are reported without repeated runs, variance, or significance estimates, despite neural SLAM commonly being sensitive to initialization and frame sampling. This makes it difficult to determine whether several improvements are robust.

Experimental comparisons are incomplete and sometimes overclaimed. Replica results are mostly aggregated rather than reported per scene; ScanNet evaluates only six sequences; different ablations use different datasets; and there is no robustness analysis for lighting changes, low texture, depth noise, dynamics, or viewpoint changes—the motivating failure conditions. The statement that both variants consistently outperform all existing methods is also too strong: the NeRF variant trails PLGSLAM on ScanNet and Point-SLAM on some Replica reconstruction metrics.

The efficiency evidence is not adequate for the added DINO/SSE machinery. Table 6 reports only one Replica scene, does not state whether online DINO extraction and SSE processing are included in FPS, defines memory as encoder/decoder footprint rather than peak runtime memory, and does not compare each base implementation directly with its DINO-augmented version. The reported 0.61 FPS for 3DGS and 2.55 FPS for NeRF on an A100 also limit practical online use.

Novelty and attribution are insufficiently positioned. The related-work section focuses on neural scene representations but does not substantively compare against feature-field, distilled-feature, semantic, or open-vocabulary mapping literature. Consequently, the broad assertion that prior implicit and explicit SLAM methods overlook such features, and the description of the two integrations as foundational paradigms, are not convincingly supported.

Important implementation information is missing: DINO checkpoint and patch configuration, selected transformer layer/token, whether it is frozen, SSE layer widths and feature dimensions, attention layout, loss normalization, optimizer and learning rates, iteration counts, sampling counts, keyframe/window parameters, Gaussian feature storage, and training/runtime treatment of the encoder. No code or reproducibility commitment is stated. These omissions are substantial because they prevent faithful reconstruction of the method and obscure whether the comparisons share identical base pipelines.

The method still relies on an offline-pretrained DINO model, so the repeated claim of operating “without offline training” is misleading unless explicitly qualified as requiring no task-specific or scene-specific offline training. Limitations are barely discussed beyond future loop closure and submapping; scalability, pretrained-model bias/domain shift, compute cost, and failure modes are not analyzed.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving dense RGB-D SLAM using self-supervised visual features without requiring semantic labels or predefined categories.

Applying a common feature-informed design to both implicit NeRF and explicit 3DGS representations is useful, and Table 4 suggests that the idea can also be incorporated into hash-grid and neural-point systems.

Evaluation covers three established datasets and considers reconstruction, rendering, tracking, runtime, and memory. Several results are favorable, including Replica completion and LPIPS, ScanNet tracking relative to several 3DGS baselines, and TUM average ATE.
The raw-DINO and EDINO ablations provide some evidence that the proposed feature supervision contributes beyond the underlying SLAM architectures.
weaknesses: Evaluated as an Algorithms/General submission because no contribution type is declared. The Scene Structure Encoder is insufficiently specified and its equations appear dimensionally problematic. In Eq. 7, a spatial tri-plane is directly compared with image-space EDINO features without defining projection, sampling, resolution alignment, or feature dimensions. In the 3DGS branch, concatenated EDINO features are rendered in Eq. 12 but supervised against raw DINO features in Eq. 14, again without explaining how their dimensions or semantics agree. These omissions prevent a convincing assessment or reproduction of the method.

The central claims of hierarchical scene understanding, part-whole relations, and structural reasoning are asserted rather than demonstrated. There is no semantic or structural evaluation, feature visualization, probing experiment, correspondence analysis, or comparison showing that EDINO encodes these properties. The reported SLAM gains alone do not establish the claimed mechanism.

The novelty appears limited to combining DINO, shallow MLPs, attention, and feature reconstruction losses with existing SLAM pipelines. The paper does not adequately position this against semantic/feature-aware neural SLAM, despite using SNI-SLAM in experiments, nor isolate what is conceptually new beyond adding learned feature channels and supervision.

Experimental gains are often modest and lack uncertainty estimates or repeated-run statistics: for example, Replica 3DGS improves PSNR from 38.94 to 39.12 and RMSE from 0.32 to 0.30, while its SSIM is below Gaussian-SLAM. On ScanNet, the NeRF average ATE is 7.1 versus ESLAM's 7.4 and remains worse than PLGSLAM's 6.8. Claims of broad or consistent superiority are therefore overstated.

Baseline comparability is unclear. The proposed 3DGS pipeline adds co-visibility keyframe selection and global bundle adjustment borrowed from another system, while comparisons are made to systems without a matched implementation of these components. Table 5 confirms that bundle adjustment has a large effect, but the paper does not provide a controlled baseline with identical tracking, mapping, and BA machinery and only the DINO component changed across the main benchmarks.

Important implementation details are missing, including the exact DINO checkpoint and extracted layer, whether it is frozen, feature resolutions and dimensions, attention tensor organization, SSE initialization and optimization schedule, total objectives and weights, iteration counts, and how features are assigned to newly created Gaussians. The claim of requiring no offline training is also ambiguous because the training of the new MLP and attention modules is not clearly described.

The mathematical presentation is incomplete or inconsistent with the stated models. Eq. 10 replaces the previously introduced anisotropic covariance with an isotropic radius, the NeRF transmittance equations omit the sampling interval, and softmax axes and tensor shapes in Eqs. 2–3 are unspecified. These are substantive ambiguities rather than minor exposition issues.

The evaluation omits robustness tests central to practical SLAM, such as sensor noise, motion blur, illumination changes, dynamic objects, and long-term loop closure. Replica results are reported only as averages, qualitative evidence is limited, and no failure cases are discussed. Runtime and memory accounting also does not clarify whether DINO extraction and feature-storage overhead are fully included.

Overall, the idea is plausible and the tables contain encouraging results, but the underspecified method, unsupported representation claims, incremental novelty, and insufficiently controlled experiments leave important concerns that favor rejection.

strengths: Assessed as an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: incorporating self-supervised visual features into dense RGB-D SLAM rather than relying exclusively on color and depth residuals.

The proposed Scene Structure Encoder combines DINO, appearance, and depth cues and is instantiated in both implicit NeRF and explicit 3D Gaussian Splatting pipelines. Supporting both representation families broadens the contribution beyond a single backend.

The evaluation covers three established benchmarks—Replica, ScanNet, and TUM—and considers reconstruction, rendering, tracking, runtime, and memory. Results are generally competitive, with particularly strong completion on Replica and average tracking accuracy on TUM.

The generality study is valuable: adding the proposed DINO machinery to hash-grid, tri-plane, neural-point, and Gaussian systems consistently improves their reported results. Component ablations also indicate that EDINO provides benefits beyond raw DINO features.
The paper is concise and visually clear, and its qualitative comparisons show plausible improvements in reconstruction completeness, fine structures, and rendered boundaries.
weaknesses: The central claims that EDINO captures hierarchical scene elements, structural relationships, and part-whole organization are not directly evaluated. All reported downstream metrics concern geometry, rendering, or pose estimation; feature visualizations, correspondence tests, semantic probing, or robustness analyses would be needed to substantiate the claimed representation properties.

Several method details are insufficiently specified for reproduction, including feature tensor resolutions and dimensions, attention layout, MLP architectures, DINO layer/token selection, online optimization of the SSE, loss aggregation, and complete training schedules. The manuscript also does not state that code will be released.

The 3DGS formulation is technically unclear. Equation 10 describes an isotropic Gaussian despite the preceding anisotropic parameterization and does not show how EDINO changes the Gaussian itself. Equations 12 and 14 appear to render EDINO-associated features but supervise them using raw DINO features, without explaining how their dimensions are reconciled.

Some conclusions are stronger than the evidence. Improvements in the generality study are often modest, no multi-run variance or significance is reported, and the comparisons mix different base architectures and evaluation metrics. It is also unclear which baselines were rerun under identical conditions versus taken from prior work.

The ablation does not fully isolate the proposed representation from other engineering choices. In particular, global bundle adjustment is an important contributor to the 3DGS tracking result, while that pipeline reportedly tracks using only color and depth residuals; consequently, the mechanism by which DINO improves pose estimation needs clearer analysis.

Efficiency reporting needs clarification about whether DINO extraction and all SSE computation are included in FPS and memory. The NeRF version is also slower and larger than its direct tri-plane baseline, which should be discussed as a practical tradeoff.

The evaluation is limited to static indoor RGB-D datasets. Robustness under appearance changes, weak texture, noisy or missing depth, dynamic objects, and longer trajectories is not studied, despite motivating the method through practical autonomous navigation.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem and proposes a simple, potentially useful mechanism for combining DINOv2 appearance features with RGB-D geometry. Its demonstrated compatibility with hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, and 2D Gaussian surfels suggests broad applicability rather than dependence on one scene representation.

The experimental scope is substantial: the method is evaluated on Replica, ScanNet, and TUM, and both implicit and explicit SLAM variants are compared with many recent systems. The GS variant reports particularly strong Replica rendering and depth results (41.42 PSNR and 0.12 cm depth L1 versus 40.25 and 0.43 for GauS-SLAM), while the ScanNet and TUM tracking averages are competitive.

Table 2 usefully separates vanilla DINO, direct DINO-depth concatenation, and the proposed geoDINO module. The consistent advantage of geoDINO provides some evidence that the attention-based fusion contributes beyond simply adding DINO features or depth channels.

The paper includes qualitative comparisons, a depth-noise experiment, integration studies across seven baselines, and runtime/memory breakdowns. These analyses are valuable for an Algorithms/General contribution and expose meaningful practical trade-offs.
weaknesses: The central technical mechanism is insufficiently specified and contains apparent inconsistencies. Equation 6 directly compares a 3D tri-plane representation with an image-space geoDINO map without defining projection, sampling, resolution, or channel alignment. For GS, the procedure that assigns image features to persistent Gaussians across frames is not described. Equation 9 claims an anisotropic covariance-based Gaussian but instead gives an isotropic radius formulation, while Equations 11–13 leave the relationship between geoDINO and vanilla-DINO feature dimensions unclear. These omissions prevent confident assessment and reproduction.

The claimed geometry awareness is only established indirectly through downstream SLAM metrics. Because SGE is optimized online jointly with the representation, its geoDINO target is itself learned and may form a moving-target or degenerate solution. There is no direct feature analysis, geometric correspondence/probing task, or visualization showing that SGE actually encodes 3D relationships. Controls such as depth-only attention, DINO attention without depth, frozen or random features, and parameter-matched extra-capacity baselines are also absent.

Experimental reproducibility is weak. The manuscript omits SGE layer widths, feature dimensions and selected DINO layers/tokens, attention details, optimizer and learning rates, iteration budgets, most loss weights, initialization, feature-resolution handling, and precise integration settings for each of the seven host systems. The project-page field is empty in the submitted manuscript, so code or configurations cannot presently resolve these gaps.

The evaluation protocol is not sufficiently controlled for the strongest claims. It is unclear which Replica frames are used to optimize the scene and which are used for rendering evaluation, despite describing the results as novel-view synthesis. Many comparison values appear collected from prior papers, but differences in implementations, preprocessing, culling, iteration budgets, and hardware are not analyzed. There are no repeated runs, uncertainty estimates, or per-scene Replica results; several headline pose gains are only 0.01 cm and may be within run-to-run variance.

Originality is moderate rather than high: prior work already integrates DINO/DINOv2 or semantic features into neural and Gaussian SLAM. The main novelty is a relatively simple two-stage attention fusion with depth plus its transplantation into existing pipelines. The broad integration study is valuable, but the paper does not isolate this mechanism rigorously enough to show that its gains arise from the proposed geometric reasoning rather than additional capacity and feature supervision.

The practical cost is understated. The NeRF implementation drops from 4.62 to 2.55 FPS and grows from 27.2 to 48.7 MB, while the GS implementation operates at only 0.58 FPS. Thus the system is not real-time on the reported hardware, and the statement that SGE adds negligible overhead is not accurate across the presented variants. Overall, the promising breadth and results make the decision close, but the technical underspecification and insufficiently controlled evidence slightly favor rejection.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant computer-vision problem: improving dense RGB-D SLAM by transferring DINOv2 features into both implicit NeRF and explicit Gaussian-splatting scene representations.

The breadth of the empirical study is a positive aspect. Table 1 applies the proposed extension to seven configurations spanning hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, and 2D surfels, and reports consistent improvements over the respective backbones.

The component ablation in Table 2 compares no DINO, vanilla DINO, simple DINO-depth concatenation, and geoDINO. The results support the narrower empirical conclusion that the proposed fusion performs better than merely attaching vanilla DINO features on Replica.

The evaluation covers Replica, ScanNet, and TUM and includes tracking, reconstruction, rendering, depth-noise, runtime, and memory measurements. The reported GS results are particularly strong, including 41.42 dB PSNR and 0.05 cm ATE RMSE on Replica.
The paper is generally well organized, and its diagrams clearly communicate the intended high-level integration into NeRF- and GS-based pipelines.
weaknesses: The technical specification is not sufficiently precise to validate or reproduce the main method. For example, Eq. 6 directly compares a 3D tri-plane representation with a 2D geoDINO feature map without defining projection, sampling, dimensional alignment, or aggregation. The token dimensions and spatial correspondence in Eqs. 2–3 are also omitted. For the GS variant, the procedure that associates every Gaussian with a feature-map embedding is described only informally and does not explain visibility conflicts, updates across frames, or feature dimensionality.

The central claim that SGE learns meaningful 3D geometry awareness is inadequately established. SGE receives depth, but the paper supplies neither an explicit 3D/geometric objective nor a diagnostic evaluation of the learned features. Because SGE is optimized online through downstream feature losses, the reported SLAM gains alone do not demonstrate that it captures the claimed structural relationships. Comparisons against stronger depth-fusion alternatives, learned RGB-D encoders, parameter-matched attention modules, and DINO features combined with existing geometric encodings are missing.

The evidence lacks statistical rigor. Tables report only single aggregate numbers, with no repeated runs, variance, confidence intervals, or significance analysis despite generally small tracking differences—for example, 0.06 to 0.05 cm on Replica and 1.54 to 1.42 cm on TUM. This is particularly important for optimization-based SLAM systems whose results can vary with initialization and frame sampling.

Evaluation protocols are underspecified. The paper does not clearly define the held-out-view protocol for rendering, trajectory-alignment procedure, number of trials, treatment of failed runs, or whether all baselines were rerun under identical settings. Table 1 even mixes different metrics across backbones, while the state-of-the-art tables appear to combine reported results from heterogeneous implementations. Consequently, the claimed rankings and broad generality are difficult to assess fairly.

Reproducibility is poor. Essential details are absent, including feature/channel sizes, MLP and attention architecture, normalization, positional information, feature-map resolution, optimizer and learning rates, iteration counts, loss weights beyond a small subset, initialization, sampling details, and precise modifications required for each of the seven backbones. No code or usable project link is supplied in the manuscript.

The novelty is modest for an Algorithms/General submission. The method mainly adds depth-conditioned cross-attention and feature-distillation losses to existing SLAM backbones. Prior DINO-informed neural representations and SLAM methods are cited, but the paper does not experimentally isolate a sufficiently distinctive principle beyond conventional RGB-D feature fusion.

Efficiency claims are overstated and accounting is unclear. The NeRF version falls from 4.62 to 2.55 FPS and grows from 27.2 to 48.7 MB, while the GS system runs at only 0.58 FPS. It is unclear whether memory and runtime include the frozen DINOv2 extractor and all feature storage. Calling the overhead broadly negligible is inconsistent with the NeRF measurements.

Robustness is tested only by adding one synthetic Gaussian-noise setting to one Replica scene. There is no evaluation of missing or biased depth, real sensor artifacts, dynamic objects, illumination changes, outdoor scenes, loop closure, or tracking failures. The qualitative comparison is also limited to selected crops without systematic failure-case analysis.

Overall, the manuscript contains promising empirical observations, but the combination of an incremental mechanism, major specification gaps, weakly controlled comparisons, and insufficient evidence for the claimed geometry-aware interpretation prevents a convincing scientific case in its current form.

strengths: As an Algorithms/General contribution, the paper presents a useful, broadly applicable strategy for injecting geometry-aware DINOv2 features into both implicit NeRF-based and explicit Gaussian-splatting RGB-D SLAM systems. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/review_acl_eccv_cvpr_han_medium_20260919T103820Z/scratch/d337b56f1f684ea7b97023452399ee5c/work/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}

The empirical scope is a major strength: the method is integrated with hash grids, tri-planes, neural points, 3D Gaussians, and 2D Gaussian surfels, producing consistent improvements across seven representative configurations.

Evaluation covers Replica, ScanNet, and TUM with tracking, reconstruction, rendering, memory, and runtime metrics. The GS variant is particularly convincing on Replica, improving GauS-SLAM from 40.25 to 41.42 PSNR and reducing depth L1 from 0.43 cm to 0.12 cm.

The ablation comparing no DINO, vanilla DINO, direct DINO-depth concatenation, and geoDINO supports the central claim that learned geometry-aware fusion is more effective than simply adding foundation-model features.
The method is clearly motivated and generally well presented, with informative diagrams, qualitative comparisons, a depth-noise experiment, and an explicit accounting of computational overhead.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is moderate: the core mechanism is an attention-based fusion of DINO and depth features followed by feature supervision of established SLAM backbones. The principal contribution is therefore the general design and empirical validation rather than a fundamentally new SLAM formulation.

The evidence does not completely isolate why SGE works. There is no depth-only or parameter-matched control, limited comparison against alternative fusion modules, and the direct DINO-depth concatenation baseline is reported only for the NeRF pipeline. Architectural ablations of the two attention stages would strengthen the causal case.

Reproducibility is limited by missing details such as feature dimensions and resolutions, precise SGE/MLP architectures, optimization schedules and iteration counts, sampling settings, complete loss weights, and method-specific integration details for the seven backbones.

SLAM results can vary across runs, but the paper reports no repeated-run statistics or uncertainty. It is also unclear whether every baseline was rerun under identical hardware and evaluation settings or partly sourced from prior publications.

Some efficiency language is optimistic: the NeRF configuration drops from 4.62 to 2.55 FPS and grows from 27.2 to 48.7 MB. Reported memory also appears narrower than total operational GPU memory, making deployment cost difficult to assess.

The robustness and generalization analyses remain limited: depth noise is tested on only one Replica scene with one synthetic noise level, TUM uses three sequences, and the system is not evaluated under dynamic content, missing depth, outdoor conditions, or loop closures. These are meaningful limitations but do not overturn the strong in-scope results.
